column2: Evidence-based beta-blockers cut mortality by about a third in chronic HFrEF (start low when euvolaemic). They are harmful in acute LVF and cardiogenic shock.
AF rate control without heart failure: a beta-blocker or rate-limiting CCB first (target < 110/min). Her CHA2DS2-VASc is 3, so anticoagulate too.
Oral anticoagulants cut AF stroke by ~two-thirds; apixaban beat warfarin with less bleeding (ARISTOTLE). Aspirin is not recommended.
Dipyridamole inhibits platelet phosphodiesterase and adenosine reuptake (raises cAMP). Clopidogrel, prasugrel and ticagrelor block P2Y12.
Mortality benefit in HFrEF is proven for bisoprolol, carvedilol and metoprolol succinate (MERIT-HF); short-acting metoprolol tartrate was inferior.
GTN is mainly a venodilator: its benefit is preload (not afterload) reduction. Avoid in hypotension, RV infarction and after PDE-5 inhibitors.
NSAIDs block renal prostaglandins, causing salt retention that blunts ACEi; with a diuretic they form the 'triple whammy' for AKI.
ACE inhibitors cause dry cough in 10–15% (bradykinin accumulation), often weeks after starting; switch to an ARB.
Dipyridamole is a phosphodiesterase inhibitor that also blocks adenosine reuptake; MR dipyridamole + aspirin is used after TIA/stroke if clopidogrel is not tolerated.
Tirofiban (like eptifibatide, abciximab) blocks platelet GP IIb/IIIa, the final common pathway of aggregation; now mainly bail-out during PCI.
Clarithromycin strongly inhibits CYP3A4, raising simvastatin levels and risking rhabdomyolysis; withhold the statin during the course.
Exertional syncope in a young person suggests structural disease (HCM, AS, anomalous coronaries); echocardiography is the key test.
BLS is support of airway, breathing and circulation without equipment: call for help, CPR 30:2 and early AED. Drugs belong to ALS.
PEA is non-shockable: CPR, adrenaline 1 mg ASAP then every 3–5 min, and treat the 4 Hs and 4 Ts (e.g. hypoxia, hypothermia).
Atrial myxoma (75% left atrial, from the septum) can obstruct the mitral valve, embolise and cause fever/high ESR (IL-6); excise surgically.
The commonest primary cardiac tumour in adults is myxoma, a pedunculated LA mass on the septum; metastases are commoner overall.
In China-like populations, as CVD peaks, stroke mortality exceeds coronary mortality (high hypertension and salt intake).
The RA lies ~5 cm below the sternal angle, so venous pulsation above the clavicle when sitting upright means a raised JVP.
Pulse amplification makes systolic pressure higher and diastolic lower in distal arteries (leg SBP > arm, basis of the ABPI).
Normal conduction: SA node → atria → AV node → His bundle → bundle branches → Purkinje fibres → ventricles (endocardium to epicardium).
The P wave is atrial depolarisation; atrial repolarisation is hidden in the PR segment/QRS. T = ventricular repolarisation.
Normal QRS axis is −30° to +90°, so −20° is normal; −30° to −90° is left axis deviation.
Sinus rhythm with normal axis, intervals, R-wave progression and no ST shift or tall T waves: a normal ECG.
SA node cells depolarise spontaneously in phase 4 (funny current) faster than any other tissue, so they reach threshold first and dominate.
Multifocal/sinus tachycardia driven by pain, dehydration and hypoxia after a hip fracture: treat the cause (analgesia, IV fluids, oxygen).
Missed dialysis with a sine-wave ECG is pre-terminal hyperkalaemia: IV calcium, insulin–glucose and salbutamol, then urgent dialysis.
A denervated transplanted heart lacks vagal tone, so it runs at its intrinsic rate (~90–110/min) and responds only to circulating catecholamines.
Late after transplant, breathlessness without angina suggests cardiac allograft vasculopathy (denervated heart); diagnose by angiography.
Lymphatic filariasis (Wuchereria bancrofti) is the commonest cause of secondary lymphoedema worldwide; cancer treatment in high-income countries.
Lymphoedema is protein-rich fluid, so diuretics do not help. Use decongestive therapy, compression, skin care and exercise.
PEA from massive haemorrhage will not reverse without volume: give blood products rapidly via the major haemorrhage protocol during CPR.
Sharp localised pain reproduced by palpation with normal ECG and CXR is musculoskeletal (costochondritis); no further tests, reassure and analgesia.
HFrEF on ACEi, beta-blocker and MRA: add an SGLT2 inhibitor (dapagliflozin), which cuts CV death and admissions with or without diabetes.
EF ≤ 30% > 40 days after MI: a primary-prevention ICD reduces mortality (MADIT-II). CRT needs LBBB with QRS ≥ 150 ms.
A resting rate of ~90/min in a well heart-transplant recipient is expected (denervation); reassure.
A donor heart tolerates only about 4 h of cold ischaemia, so it must be allocated within a limited radius of the donor.
In transplant-ineligible stage D heart failure, a durable LVAD (destination therapy) improves survival; inotropes do not.
CHD affects ~1% of births and ~90% of neonates now survive, so adults with CHD now outnumber children.
A flap that opens intermittently between atria is a PFO (~25% of adults), allowing paradoxical embolism; no treatment if incidental.
A small restrictive VSD with Qp:Qs < 1.5 and normal pulmonary pressures needs no closure; review periodically and maintain dental hygiene.
A coronary sinus saturation of 91% (normally ~30–40%) means arterial blood is entering it: a coronary AV fistula, causing a continuous murmur and steal.
Bicuspid aortic valve carries an aortopathy, so measure the aortic root/ascending aorta on every echo; repair at 55 mm (50 mm with risk factors).
Tetralogy of Fallot: VSD, overriding aorta, RVOT obstruction and RV hypertrophy. Tricuspid atresia is a separate cyanotic lesion.
Calcific AS of a trileaflet valve at 78 shares atherosclerotic risk factors: age, diabetes, hypertension, smoking, lipids, CKD.
Untreated severe AS: average survival ~5 years after angina, 3 after syncope and 2 after heart failure; any symptom means valve replacement.
